Solution

Designing clinical and patient-facing experiences where clarity, trust, and compliance are non-negotiable.

Healthcare products must be accurate under pressure, compliant with regulation, and usable by people whose primary job is not using software. The design constraints are strict and the stakes are real — which makes good design both harder and more important.

Payor

HIPAA

Privacy-aware IA and access patterns

Real

Clinical research and user testing experience

The challenge

The challenge with healthcare products

Clinical workflows are complex, time-constrained, and high-stakes. The users — clinicians, care coordinators, billing staff — are expert practitioners who need software that respects their expertise and gets out of their way. Most healthcare software does the opposite: it demands attention, requires workarounds, and generates the kind of alert fatigue that creates real risk.

Patient-facing products have a different but related problem: they must translate clinical complexity into language that non-specialist users can act on — accurately, without oversimplifying, and under conditions of anxiety and uncertainty.

My approach

How I design for healthcare

I design for high-stakes environments by reducing cognitive load at the moment of decision. The goal is not to simplify the domain — healthcare is genuinely complex — but to surface the right information at the right moment, with the right emphasis, so users can act correctly without having to fight the interface.

Safeguards against common errors are designed as part of the flow, not bolted on as warning dialogs. Compliance requirements are treated as design constraints from the start, not reviewed at the end. And accessibility is non-negotiable — clinical settings include users with visual, motor, and cognitive needs that must be accommodated.

Key Patterns

How this shows up in the work.

Clinical workflow mapping

Deep research into real clinical workflows — not idealized process diagrams, but the actual sequence of steps under real time pressure.

Alert fatigue reduction

Designing notification hierarchies that reserve high-attention alerts for genuinely high-priority events — and make low-priority information scannable, not interruptive.

Error prevention by design

Confirmation patterns, undo affordances, and input validation designed to catch common errors before they propagate — not after.

HIPAA-aware IA

Information architecture that respects data sensitivity: what is shown by default, what requires explicit access, and how PHI is surfaced in context.

Accessibility in clinical settings

WCAG 2.1 AA compliance as a baseline, with attention to clinical-specific needs: high-contrast modes for poor lighting, large tap targets for gloved hands.

Patient-facing translation

Designing clinical information for lay users: plain language, progressive complexity, and decision-support patterns that inform without overwhelming.
